blocks.text: The endosymbiotic theory was proposed by Lynn Margulis. According to it, large prokaryotes engulfed small prokaryotes, which were not digested but lived inside the large cells and evolved into organelles. The partners formed a symbiotic relationship that benefited both.

items: Some small prokaryotes could carry out aerobic respiration; they supplied energy to themselves and to the large cell, and became mitochondria.
Other small cells could use sunlight to make food and shared it with the large cell; they became chloroplasts.
Flagella may have come from the ingestion of prokaryotes similar to spirochaetes (a more debated suggestion).

blocks.alt: Left: a large prokaryote with its DNA, approached by a small red aerobic bacterium and a small green photosynthetic bacterium. An arrow labelled engulfed, not digested leads to a eukaryotic cell containing a nucleus, endoplasmic reticulum, a red mitochondrion and a green chloroplast. A box lists the evidence.
blocks.caption: Endosymbiosis and the origin of eukaryotic cells (original diagram after Figure 24.6).
blocks.long_description: According to Lynn Margulis's endosymbiotic theory, large prokaryotes engulfed smaller ones without digesting them, and the two came to live together to the benefit of both. Small cells that carried out aerobic respiration supplied energy and became mitochondria; small cells that used sunlight to make food became chloroplasts. Evidence: mitochondria and chloroplasts are about the size of prokaryotes, have their own circular DNA like a prokaryotic chromosome, divide by binary fission, and have membranes more like those of prokaryotes. The membrane invagination theory adds that infolding of the cell membrane formed internal membranes such as the nucleus and endoplasmic reticulum.

blocks.text: Eukaryotic cells formed by endosymbiosis were powerful and efficient, which let them evolve new features such as multicellularity, cell specialisation and large size; they were the key to the great diversity of animals, plants and fungi today.

blocks.title: Evidence for the endosymbiotic theory
blocks.text: Mitochondria and chloroplasts are about the size of prokaryotic cells; they have their own DNA in a circular chromosome like that of prokaryotes; they reproduce by binary fission like prokaryotes, whereas eukaryotic cells divide by mitosis; and their membranes are more like prokaryotic than eukaryotic membranes.

blocks.title: Membrane invagination theory
blocks.text: Another theory says that the cell membrane of a prokaryotic cell folded inward into the cytoplasm, giving rise to membranous structures such as the nucleus and endoplasmic reticulum, and so to a eukaryotic cell.
